t.5.32.2: O Devī, I have come to you as a messenger at Rāma's command. O Vaidehī, Rāma is well, and he has asked about your welfare.
t.5.32.1: Having heard those words of hers, who was overwhelmed by sorrow upon sorrow, Hanūmān, leader of the monkey troops, spoke a comforting reply.
t.5.32.4: And Lakṣmaṇa too, the greatly radiant one, the beloved companion of your husband, burning with grief, has offered you his salutation with bowed head.
t.5.32.3: O Devī, Rāma, son of Daśaratha, who knows the Brahmā weapon and the Vedas and is foremost among those who know the Vedas, has asked after your welfare.
t.5.32.5: Having heard of the well-being of those two lions among men, the queen, every limb of her thrilling with joy, then spoke to Hanūmān.
t.5.32.6: Auspicious indeed this popular saying seems to me: 'Come, joy, to the man who stays alive, even after a hundred years!'
t.5.32.7: At that meeting of the two, a wondrous affection arose, and the two, having gained trust, conversed with one another.
t.5.32.8: Having heard those words of hers, Hanūmān, leader of the monkey troops, approached Sītā, who was wretched with grief.
t.5.32.9: The nearer Hanūmān drew to her, the more Sītā suspected him of being Rāvaṇa.
t.5.32.11: Letting go of that branch of the aśoka tree, she of flawless limbs, worn thin by grief, sat down upon that very ground.
t.5.32.10: Alas, shame, shame on what I have done, for I have told all this to him! Having taken on another form, this is surely that very Rāvaṇa.
t.5.32.12: Then the mighty-armed one paid homage to her, the daughter of Janaka; and she, terrified with fear, did not look up at him again.
t.5.32.13: Seeing him bowing in reverence, Sītā, whose face was like the moon, sighed deeply and spoke to the monkey in a sweet voice.
t.5.32.14: If you are Rāvaṇa himself, the master of illusion, who has entered into a magical disguise, and you cause me fresh anguish once more, that is not fitting.
t.5.32.15: You who, abandoning your own form and assuming the form of a wandering ascetic, were seen by me in Janasthāna, you are that very Rāvaṇa.
t.5.32.16: O night-wanderer who takes any form at will, you torment me again, wretched and wasted by fasting as I am; such torment is not seemly.
t.5.32.17: If you have come as the messenger of Rāma, may good fortune be yours! I question you, O best of monkeys, for talk of Rāma is dear to me.
t.5.32.18: Tell me of the virtues of my beloved Rāma, O monkey; you carry away my heart, gentle one, as a river's current carries away its bank.
t.5.32.19: Oh, the sweetness of this dream, that I, carried off so long ago, should see a forest-dweller sent, as it seems, by Rāghava!
t.5.32.20: If I could see the heroic Rāghava together with Lakṣmaṇa even in a dream, I would not lose heart; but even sleep is jealous of me.
t.5.32.21: I do not think this is a dream, for when one has seen a monkey in a dream, good fortune cannot be attained; yet good fortune has come to me.
t.5.32.22: What can this be? Is it a delusion of the mind, or is it some disorder of the vital wind? Is it a derangement born of madness, or is it a mirage?
t.5.32.24: Thus Sītā, having weighed in many ways the strength and weakness of the matter, thought him to be the lord of the Rākṣasas, because Rākṣasas can take on any form at will.
t.5.32.23: Or rather, this is not madness, nor is it a delusion bearing the marks of madness, for I am fully aware of myself and of this forest-dweller as well.
t.5.32.25: Having then formed this thought, that slender-waisted Sītā, the daughter of Janaka, did not reply to the monkey.
t.5.32.26: Understanding what Sītā was thinking, Hanūmān, the son of Māruta, then delighted her with words pleasing to the ear.
t.5.32.27: Radiant like the sun, beloved of the world like the moon, he is king of all the world, like the god Vaiśravaṇa.
t.5.32.28: He is endowed with valour like the greatly renowned Viṣṇu, and he is truthful and sweet of speech like the god Vācaspati.
t.5.32.30: You will see the fruit that befalls him by whom you were carried off in that empty place, after he had drawn Rāghava away from the hermitage by means of a deer's form.
t.5.32.29: He is handsome, blessed and glorious, like Kandarpa in bodily form; he strikes in anger only where anger is due, and he is the foremost great chariot-warrior in the world, that great-souled one in the shade of whose arms the world finds its support.
t.5.32.31: He, the valiant one, who before long will slay Rāvaṇa in battle with arrows loosed in wrath, blazing like fires.
t.5.32.32: Sent by him as a messenger, I have come here into your presence. Afflicted with sorrow at being separated from you, he has asked after your welfare.
t.5.32.33: And the mighty-armed Lakṣmaṇa of great splendour, who increases the joy of Sumitrā, also saluted you and asked after your welfare.
t.5.32.34: And, O queen, Rāma's friend, the monkey named Sugrīva, king of the foremost of the monkeys, has asked after your welfare.
t.5.32.35: Rāma, together with Sugrīva and Lakṣmaṇa, constantly remembers you. By good fortune you are alive, O Vaidehī, though you have fallen into the power of the rākṣasīs.
t.5.32.36: Before long you will see Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, the great chariot-warrior, and Sugrīva of boundless might, in the midst of tens of millions of monkeys.
t.5.32.37: I am a monkey named Hanūmān, the minister of Sugrīva; having leapt across the great ocean, I have entered the city of Laṅkā.
t.5.32.38: Having set my foot upon the head of the evil-souled Rāvaṇa, I have come here to see you, relying on my own valour.
t.5.32.39: I am not such as you take me to be, O queen. Let this suspicion be abandoned; put your faith in me as I speak.
